items.prompt: Identify the main features of a trade union.
items.canonical_answer: A trade union is an organisation of workers, not of firms or the government. Membership is voluntary, and members' subscriptions fund it. It negotiates with employers for its members as one body. It aims to protect and improve members' pay and working conditions.
marking_guidance: Features: what it includes - the four features (an organisation of workers, voluntary subscription-paying members, speaking as one body, the aim on pay and working conditions) are each named distinctly.

items.canonical_answer: Collective bargaining is negotiation between a trade union and an employer over the pay and working conditions of the union's members, with the union speaking for all of them as one body.
marking_guidance: Precise definition required: the meaning must state the union negotiating with the employer on behalf of its members as a single body, over pay and working conditions.

items.prompt: Explain why workers may choose to join a trade union.
items.canonical_answer: A worker bargaining alone has little weight, because an employer can replace one worker more easily than a whole workforce. A union negotiates for all its members at once, so each member tends to have more influence over pay and conditions. Members are also represented in disputes with the employer, such as an unfair dismissal, and the union presses for safer workplaces and training. So the subscription buys strength in numbers, protection at work and a voice a lone worker usually lacks.
marking_guidance: Reason: each purpose - more weight in bargaining as one body, representation in disputes, protection of pay and conditions - is given with the reason it matters to a worker, because the question asks why workers join.

items.prompt: At Kuiseb Fish Processors, a cannery in Walvis Bay, 240 of the 300 workers belong to the Marine Workers' Union. In 2026 the union negotiated a pay rise from N$12.50 to N$14.00 an hour, and the cannery paid the higher rate to all 300 workers. Explain how this episode shows the role of a trade union in the economy.
items.canonical_answer: The union bargained collectively, winning one rise from N$12.50 to N$14.00 an hour for its 240 members. The cannery settled because losing 240 workers at once would stop the plant. Because it paid the new rate to all 300 workers, the union raised pay beyond its own members. Pay agreed at a large workplace also tends to spread, because nearby employers competing for the same workers are likely to match it. Therefore the episode shows a union influencing wages across the labour market, not only at one firm.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the figures from the extract - the 240 members among 300 workers and the rise from N$12.50 to N$14.00 an hour - since the question asks how this episode shows the role.
Reasoning: the link from collective bargaining to the pay rise and its spread beyond members must be explained, because naming the rise alone is not an explanation.
Conclusion: therefore the answer closes on what the episode means for the union's role in the wider economy - pay lifted beyond one workplace.

items.prompt: The Textile Workers' Union at Oshakati Textiles has negotiated a pay rise from N$11.00 to N$12.10 an hour for the firm's 500 machinists. Discuss the likely effects of this union-negotiated pay rise on the firm, its workers and the town's economy.
items.canonical_answer: The union has raised hourly pay from N$11.00 to N$12.10, an increase of N$12.10 - N$11.00 = N$1.10. Because each machinist's hour now costs N$1.10 more, the labour cost of every garment rises, so the firm must raise prices, accept lower profit or employ fewer machinists. A machinist working 45 hours a week earns N$1.10 x 45 = N$49.50 more, and much of it is likely to be spent in Oshakati's shops, so local traders gain. If the firm's buyers can switch to cheaper imports, it may not be able to raise prices, so it may leave posts unfilled when machinists leave, and jobs in the town may fall over time. If better pay lifts motivation and fewer workers leave, the firm saves on recruiting and training. The machinists gain income, the owners bear the higher cost, traders gain sales and consumers may pay more. The overall effect depends on whether the firm's sales can carry the cost.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial change - the negotiated rise from N$11.00 to N$12.10 an hour - is stated first, and when it is given the arithmetic is shown.
Mechanism: because the hourly labour cost rises, this causes the firm's response and the workers' gain, each traced through the cost chain.
Consequence: therefore the results for prices, employment and local trade must each be traced to a named outcome, and results in opposite directions are both credited.
For whom: the winners and losers are named - workers, the firm and its owners, local traders, consumers - and the economy-wide effect on the town is drawn out.

items.canonical_answer: Industrial action is action taken by union members together to put pressure on an employer, such as refusing to work at all (a strike), refusing to work beyond set duties (work-to-rule), or refusing overtime.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must state action by union members acting together to pressure the employer, with at least one form, such as a strike or work-to-rule, named.

items.prompt: Explain why trade union activity may reduce a firm's costs even though it raises the firm's pay bill.
items.canonical_answer: The negotiated rise increases the wage bill, but union activity can lower other costs. When the union secures safer workplaces and clearer conditions, there are fewer disputes, so the firm loses fewer days to stoppages. Workers who feel fairly paid tend to stay, so the firm spends less on recruiting and training replacements. A settled relationship also keeps production steady, so the firm is less likely to miss deliveries. Whether total costs fall depends on whether these savings outweigh the higher pay bill.
marking_guidance: Reason: the purpose of each saving - fewer stoppages, lower turnover of staff, steadier production - is linked to a cost it avoids, because the question asks why costs may fall while the pay bill rises.

items.prompt: In March 2026, 180 members of the Meat Workers' Union at Marula Meat Processors, an abattoir in Gobabis, stopped work for three days over a pay dispute, and the abattoir lost output it valued at N$96 000. After talks with the union the hourly pay rate rose from N$10.00 to N$11.00, and the union agreed to two years without a strike. Explain, using the figures, the effects of this union activity on the business.
items.canonical_answer: The union's activity brought the abattoir a cost and a benefit. The three-day stoppage lost output worth N$96 000, and the settlement raised pay by N$11.00 - N$10.00 = N$1.00 an hour for every hour the 180 members work. Because the union agreed to two years without a strike, the abattoir can plan production and meet orders with more confidence, and better-paid workers are more likely to stay. Therefore the figures show a cost during the dispute and a benefit from the agreement that protects future output.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer uses the figures from the extract - the N$96 000 of lost output, the three stoppage days, and the rise from N$10.00 to N$11.00 an hour.
Reasoning: each effect is linked back to the union action and its settlement, because a cost or benefit stated without the link earns nothing.
Conclusion: therefore the answer weighs the cost of the stoppage against the benefit of the no-strike agreement, which means that both faces of the activity are drawn.

items.prompt: Workers at Bay Cold Storage in Walvis Bay work 11-hour shifts with no extra pay for long hours. Their union negotiates 9-hour shifts, with any hour beyond that paid at one and a half times the normal rate of N$30 an hour. Explain how this collective bargaining over working hours affects the workers and the firm.
items.canonical_answer: Through collective bargaining the union has cut shifts from 11 to 9 hours and won overtime pay of 1.5 x N$30 = N$45 an hour. Because each extra hour now costs N$15 more than a normal hour, the firm is likely to plan rosters to limit overtime, perhaps by hiring extra staff. Workers gain rest, safer shifts and better pay for long hours. Therefore bargaining over hours protects workers' time and health while raising the firm's labour costs.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer uses the figures - shifts cut from 11 to 9 hours and overtime at one and a half times N$30 an hour.
Reasoning: because overtime now costs more, the firm has a reason to limit it, while workers gain shorter shifts.
Conclusion: therefore workers gain rest and pay for long hours, which means higher labour costs for the firm.

items.prompt: Namib Can Works plans to make 80 of its 400 workers redundant as orders fall. Its union instead negotiates 20 voluntary redundancies and, for the 380 remaining workers, a four-day week for six months instead of five days, with pay reduced in proportion to hours. Assume equal daily wages. Analyse the consequences for workers, the firm and the town.
items.canonical_answer: The agreement keeps 380 rather than 320 workers employed, preserving 60 more jobs and spreading the loss of work. Each retained worker earns four-fifths of former weekly pay. Total weekly wages are therefore equivalent to 380 x 4/5 = 304 former full-week wages, against 320 under the original redundancy plan. Fewer jobs lost does not mean a smaller total wage-income loss. The firm retains more trained staff for recovery, but workers and local shops still face reduced income and spending. Redundancy payments may soften the immediate loss; their amount is not given.
marking_guidance: Starting point: 80 proposed redundancies are replaced by 20 voluntary departures and a four-day week for 380 retained staff.
Mechanism: because hours and pay fall to four-fifths, total weekly wages equal 380 x 4/5 = 304 former full-week wages.
Consequence: 60 more jobs remain than under the original plan, but total weekly wages are lower than 320 full-week wages.
For whom: workers share the income loss, the firm retains skills, and town shops face lower wage-funded spending; redundancy payments are unspecified.

items.prompt: Explain why trade unions try to influence government policy.
items.canonical_answer: Many things that matter to workers are set by government rather than by one employer: the national minimum wage, rules on dismissal, health and safety standards and pensions. A union that wins a better law gains it for workers in every firm the law covers, including workplaces where the union is weak. Unions also speak for many voters, which gives ministers a reason to listen. Therefore lobbying, submissions on new laws and public campaigns can protect members more widely than bargaining with one employer.
marking_guidance: Reason: the purpose is to change rules set by government, because a law reaches workers in many firms at once.
Development: the reason is linked to the methods - lobbying, submissions, campaigns - and to the weight that many members and voters give a union.

items.prompt: Identify two factors that influence the strength of a trade union.
items.canonical_answer: The share of the workforce in the union: the higher it is, the more the employer stands to lose from a strike. The state of the economy: when unemployment is low, employers find replacements harder to hire.
marking_guidance: Features: one mark per factor named, from what it includes - membership share, how hard members are to replace, unemployment, the employer's profits and demand, the law on strikes, strike funds, public support.
Each factor is credited once; two wordings of the same factor earn one mark.

items.prompt: At Khan River Uranium's mine near Arandis, 900 of the 1 000 workers belong to a union, most are skilled machine operators, and the mine is earning record profits. At a Windhoek car wash, 6 of the 40 washers belong to a union and the work can be learnt in a day. Explain why the union at the mine is likely to be stronger than the union at the car wash.
items.canonical_answer: Membership: 900 of 1 000 mine workers, 90%, belong to the union, against 6 of 40 washers, 15%, so a strike at the mine could halt output while one at the car wash would barely slow it. Skills: skilled machine operators are hard to replace, whereas washing can be learnt in a day, so the car wash can hire others. Profit: record profits mean the mine can afford a rise more readily. Therefore the mine's union is likely to win more in bargaining.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer uses the data - 900 of 1 000 against 6 of 40 members, skilled operators against work learnt in a day, and record profits.
Reasoning: because a high membership share and hard-to-replace skills raise what a strike would cost the employer, the union's bargaining weight rises.
Conclusion: therefore the mine's union is likely to be stronger, which means it can expect to win more.

items.prompt: Namibia's public service and several of its largest private employers bargain with strong trade unions. Discuss whether trade union activity is likely to be beneficial for the government.
items.canonical_answer: Why it might be: unions give the government one body to consult when it drafts labour law, so new rules are more likely to be accepted. Disputes settled at a bargaining table cost less than strikes. Pay rises for low-paid workers narrow the gap between rich and poor, which may reduce the need for state support, and higher wages bring in more income tax. Why it might not be: strikes by nurses, teachers or bus drivers stop public services the government must provide; as an employer, the government faces pay claims that add to its budget; and rises that outpace output can push up prices or lead firms to cut jobs, costing tax revenue. On balance, union activity is likely to benefit the government where bargaining stays at the table and pay rises are matched by output; what settles it is whether disputes in essential services are resolved without long strikes.
marking_guidance: Judgement: the answer reaches a supported judgement - on balance, or it depends on the condition named.
Why it might: the argument for is developed - consultation, cheaper settlement, narrower pay gaps, tax revenue.
Why it might not: the argument against is developed - strikes in public services, the public pay bill, rising prices, lost jobs.
The condition: the decisive point - what settles it - is whether bargaining stays at the table and pay rises are matched by output.

items.prompt:
Eight questions in the style of Paper 1. Choose one option for each.

1. A trade union is best defined as:
A  an organisation of firms that trades goods between countries
B  an organisation of workers, joined and funded by them, that aims to protect and improve its members' pay and working conditions
C  a government body that sets wages by law
D  a bank that lends to workers at reduced rates

2. Collective bargaining means:
A  each worker negotiating pay alone with the manager
B  the government fixing a national wage for a trade
C  the union negotiating pay and working conditions for its members as one body
D  employers meeting together to agree prices

3. Why may a worker join a trade union?
A  to receive a transfer payment from the government
B  because the union negotiates on behalf of all members, giving one worker more influence than bargaining alone
C  because the law requires workers in a factory to belong
D  to pay a lower rate of tax on income

4. A union wins a rise from N$12.50 to N$14.00 an hour. Hourly pay rises by:
A  N$1.50
B  N$2.50
C  N$12.50
D  N$26.50

5. While a strike at a cannery lasts, which effect is most likely?
A  the firm's output falls for the days of the stoppage
B  the firm's prices fall at once
C  the striking workers' pay rises
D  the government pays the striking workers' wages

6. A union negotiates safer conditions and steadier rosters. The firm may find that:
A  costs rise from the safety spending and the firm gains nothing else
B  fewer stoppages and fewer departures lower some of its other costs
C  its pay bill falls
D  its revenue rises without any change in sales

7. Trade union activity is most likely to weaken a firm's competitiveness when:
A  the pay rise it wins raises costs faster than the firm's output per worker
B  it settles disputes before they reach a stoppage
C  it lifts workers' motivation
D  its bargains spread to nearby firms

8. Which is the test that a body is a trade union rather than a trade organisation promoting a country's exports?
A  it charges its members a subscription
B  it publishes reports on the economy
C  its head office stands in a capital city
D  its members are workers and it bargains with employers over pay and conditions
items.canonical_answer:
Key: 1 B, 2 C, 3 B, 4 A, 5 A, 6 B, 7 A, 8 D.
1. B is the definition (workers joined and funded by them, protecting pay and conditions); A is trade between nations mistaken for a union, C mistakes a union for a government wage-setter, D mistakes it for a lender.
2. C is collective bargaining (union as one body for its members); A runs the negotiation worker-by-worker, B confuses a union with the government, D confuses bargaining with firms agreeing prices.
3. B gives the reason (strength in numbers); A confuses a union with a transfer payment, C treats membership as compulsory when it is voluntary, D confuses a subscription with a tax cut.
4. N$14.00 - N$12.50 = N$1.50, so A; B subtracts the wrong way, C confuses the new rate with the rise, D adds where it should subtract.
5. A stoppage halts output while it lasts (A); B reverses the price effect, C reverses who gains, D invents a payment the striking workers do not receive.
6. B names the offsets (fewer stoppages, fewer departures to replace); A denies the firm any offsetting gain, C reverses the effect on the pay bill, D confuses lower costs with automatically higher revenue.
7. A states the condition (costs rising faster than output per worker); B and C are effects that help the firm, D is a spread that is neither harm nor competitiveness in itself.
8. D is the test (members are workers, bargains with employers over pay); A fits many bodies including export promoters, B and C describe things either kind of body might do.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark per question, eight in total; the correct option for each is listed and each distractor is explained as the specific misunderstanding it catches.

Every distractor traces to a named error: a union confused with trade between nations, with the government, or with a lender; bargaining confused with individual negotiation or price-fixing; a rise confused with the new rate; a cost saving denied or reversed.

items.prompt:
A report in the Oshakati Advertiser, 2026: "The Textile Workers' Union signed a new pay deal with Oshakati Textiles in March after six strike days at the plant. Hourly pay for machinists rises from N$11.00 to N$12.10. Union membership at the plant has grown from 320 of the 400 machinists employed in 2022 to 480 of the 500 employed now. Traders in the streets near the factory gate report their best pay-day takings in years."

Table 1 - Oshakati Textiles
  machinists employed, 2022: 400
  machinists employed, 2026: 500
  union members, 2022: 320
  union members, 2026: 480
  hourly pay, 2025: N$11.00
  hourly pay, 2026: N$12.10
  strike days lost, 2026: 6

(a) Calculate the percentage of machinists who were union members in 2026. [1]
(b) Identify from Table 1 the number of strike days lost in 2026 and the hourly pay after the deal. [2]
(c) Explain why union membership at the plant may have grown between 2022 and 2026. [4]
(d) Analyse, using Table 1, the effects of the union's pay deal on the firm and on the town's economy. [6]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) 480 members among 500 machinists: 480 out of 500 is 96%, so 96% of machinists were union members in 2026.
(b) From Table 1: 6 strike days were lost in 2026, and hourly pay after the deal is N$12.10.
(c) Machinists can see what the union delivers: it has won a rise from N$11.00 to N$12.10 an hour, so joining looks like it buys something. As membership grew from 320 to 480, the union came to speak for 480 of the 500 machinists, which makes it harder for the firm to ignore and so makes membership worth more to each new member. The 100 machinists hired as the workforce grew from 400 to 500 joined a plant where most colleagues already belonged, which is likely to draw them in. Against that, a settlement at the plant tends to cover every machinist, so a worker could hope to gain while staying out; the growth from 320 to 480 members suggests the visible gains have been the stronger draw.
(d) A pay deal raises the firm's labour costs and its workers' spending, so the data should show both a cost pressure on the firm and a spending gain in the town. The deal lifts hourly pay from N$11.00 to N$12.10 and covers a membership of 480 among 500 machinists; the deal cost 6 strike days before it was signed; traders near the gate report their best pay-day takings in years. Each extra N$1.10 an hour (N$12.10 - N$11.00 = N$1.10) adds to the wage bill of every hour worked, so the firm faces a choice between dearer garments, absorbing the cost from profit, or a workforce allowed to drift down by not replacing leavers; at the same time 480 machinists on higher pay hand more income to Oshakati's traders, which is what the traders' report shows. However, where the firm's buyers can switch to cheaper imports, the cost side can outweigh the spending gain, since a plant that ships less pays out less in wages, and the employment growth from 400 to 500 machinists could stop or reverse even with the deal in place. So the deal's effect on the town depends on whether the firm's sales hold.
marking_guidance: Context: parts (a) and (b) are read from Table 1; parts (c) and (d) must use the figures - the 320 of 400 and 480 of 500 memberships, the N$11.00 to N$12.10 rise, the 6 strike days.
Reasoning: one mark per distinct linked statement; quoting a figure on its own is not analysis - the relationship must be stated and the reason given.
Conclusion: part (d) runs expected relationship, then evidence, then analysis, then an exception.
For whom: consequences are named for the firm, the machinists and the town's traders.

hourly pay N$11.00 in 2025 and N$12.10 in 2026

items.prompt:
Answer all parts.
(a) Define a trade union. [2]
(b) Explain why a worker who is not a union member may still benefit from the union's activity at their workplace. [4]
(c) Analyse the likely effects on a firm of a union-negotiated pay rise. [6]
(d) Discuss whether trade union activity benefits an economy. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) A trade union is an organisation of workers, joined and funded by them, that aims to protect and improve its members' pay and working conditions.
(b) When a union negotiates a rise, the employer often extends it to the whole workplace rather than run two pay rates side by side, so a non-member gains the higher rate while paying no subscription. Negotiated conditions - safety rules, clearer shift arrangements - tend to cover the workplace as a whole, again reaching non-members. The union's representation of members in disputes also sets a standard of treatment that spills over to colleagues. Against that, where the union's action stops production, the non-member loses the same pay for the strike days without having had a vote.
(c) The firm's hourly labour cost rises. Because producing each unit costs more in labour, the firm responds through prices, hiring, or its profit margin. Where the firm raises prices, its buyers may switch to cheaper imports and sales fall; where it cannot, it may let the workforce shrink by not replacing leavers; where it absorbs the cost, profit falls and funds for investment shrink with it. There are offsetting gains: workers who feel fairly paid tend to stay, so the firm spends less on recruitment and training, and a settled relationship with the union loses fewer days to stoppages. Owners bear the cost in profit, consumers bear it in prices, workers gain in pay, and the balance turns on whether the rise matches output per worker.
(d) Case for: unions bargain for workers who alone carry little weight, so pay at the bottom of the labour market tends to rise and the gap between low and higher pay narrows; the income won is spent, and spending supports the firms and traders around each workplace. Case against: rises won ahead of output per worker raise firms' costs, and firms facing dearer labour may raise prices or hire less, so the jobs a union protects at one plant may be lost across a town; strikes stop output and pay while they last, and the stoppage costs spread to the firm's suppliers and buyers. Judgement: the activity itself is neither good nor bad for an economy - what decides it is whether bargains track what workers produce and whether the two sides settle at a table rather than on a picket line. In a growing economy with matching output, union activity tends to help; in a weak one with rises ahead of production, it tends to harm.
marking_guidance: Parts (a) to (d) carry a model answer each; (d) is level-marked over three bands.
Context: (b) and (c) build on the workplace and the firm's costs, and the answers name the parties - non-members, owners, consumers, workers.
Reasoning: (c) one mark per distinct linked statement, the chain from the rise to prices, employment and profit traced.

Conclusion: (d) the top band examines why it might and why it might not, reaches a judgement, and names the condition the judgement depends on - whether rises match output per worker and how the two sides settle.

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: "Discuss whether a trade union should use industrial action to win a pay rise." Build the plan on the advantages and disadvantages of union activity. Do not write the essay; produce the plan.
items.canonical_answer:
Case for (strength the table lacks): a single worker's bargaining position is weak, and industrial action is the union's strongest card, because an employer who can replace one worker cannot easily replace five hundred.
Chain 1: talks stall -> members stop work -> the firm's output halts and the stoppage starts costing it money -> the employer has a reason to move that talk alone did not give (for whom: members gain bargaining power; the firm loses output).
Chain 2: action succeeds -> pay rises -> income of low-paid households rises and is spent locally (for whom: members and local traders gain; the firm pays).
Case against (what the action costs): the stoppage costs both sides from the first day.
Chain 3: members strike -> they lose pay for each strike day -> households that can least afford it carry the cost, and the employer's buyers may take their orders elsewhere for good (for whom: striking workers lose pay; the firm may lose customers permanently).
Chain 4: the rise is won ahead of output per worker -> the firm's costs rise faster than its production -> it raises prices or stops hiring -> the jobs the union defended may go over time (for whom: consumers and future job-seekers bear it).
Judgement: industrial action is a tool for a deadlock, not a first move - it tends to serve members best where talks have genuinely failed, the stoppage fund can carry the members' lost pay, and the rise sought is one the firm can fund out of the production its workers deliver.
Condition: the judgement turns on the state of the firm's sales and the union's strength - a weak firm may be pushed past the point where it can employ at all, which converts a pay dispute into a jobs dispute.
marking_guidance: A plan, not an essay: the chains and the stated judgement are what is assessed.
Criterion: the decisive factor is whether the rise sought can be paid out of what the workers produce, and whether talks have truly failed.
Counterargument: the case against must appear - lost pay for striking days, output lost to the firm, and rises won ahead of production costing jobs.
Condition: the plan must end on what would change the judgement - the firm's sales, the strength of the stoppage fund, and the state of the economy.
For whom: each chain names who gains and who loses - members, the firm, its customers, local traders, future job-seekers.
